name: Renaissance moral and religious ambivalence
plain_explanation: Renaissance Italians pursued culture and learning with great seriousness but were comparatively indifferent to morality and religion; unorthodoxy remained purely intellectual because questioning the papal system too openly threatened Italy's economic dependence on Church revenues drawn from the whole Catholic world.
precise_definition: Russell's characterization: 'The Italians were in earnest about culture, but not about morals and religion,' and Italian unorthodoxy 'was purely intellectual, and did not lead to schism, or to any attempt to create a popular movement away from the Church,' with Savonarola as the only partial exception.
why_it_mattered: Explains why the Reformation, when it came, arose in the North rather than in Italy itself, despite Italy's greater intellectual freedom.
historical_origin: Rooted in Rome's economic dependence on tribute from the wider Catholic world via the doctrine that the popes held the keys of heaven.
examples: Cardinals bringing their own wine and cup-bearers to a papal coronation for fear of poison
Innocent VIII's 1484 bull against witchcraft, leading to persecution
The revived vogue for astrology among freethinkers
competing_positions: Northern humanism (Erasmus, More), which combined learning with genuine piety and public virtue (Chapter IV)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets up the contrast Russell draws in Chapter IV between the Italian and northern Renaissances.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central: Rome's financial dependence on papal spiritual authority explains the limits of Italian free-thought.
